drafts.neutral_framing: Travis County already publishes every payment online. Should it take the next step no Texas government has — publishing item-level purchase-card spending, the way Oklahoma does?
drafts.final_wording: Travis County already publishes every vendor payment online — further than most. Should it reach the frontier no Texas government has: publishing what was actually bought, item by item?
drafts.final_wording_note: Framed around Travis’s real position: it already leads on check-level disclosure, so the meaningful question is the next tier.
shaping_notes: A policy question about disclosure format, not any person — clears the bright lines.
Grounded in fact: Travis runs a Vendor Payment Register that ties payments to invoices/POs; no Texas local government publishes item-level purchase-card data, and Oklahoma is the lone benchmark.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion.
drafts.background: Travis County is already a Texas transparency leader — its Vendor Payment Register lets anyone search every payment and see the invoices and purchase orders behind it, one of the strongest county payment portals in the state. That is the floor receipts by rails assumes as already won. The open frontier — which no Texas local government has crossed — is item-level disclosure: publishing what was actually bought, not just who was paid. Only one government does it today: Oklahoma, which posts every state purchase-card transaction, itemized.

founding_solutions.title: Pay procurement from line-attributed accounts, so the itemized receipt is native
founding_solutions.summary: Travis already publishes who got paid. The next tier is what was bought — item level. Pay discretionary/procurement spending from authorized, line-attributed accounts (virtual cards or ring-fenced accounts) whose feed publishes by default, so the itemized receipt is generated by the payment itself. It reaches ~15-30% of the budget (the operating slice), and is framed as audit and anti-diversion, not control. No Texas government does item-level purchase-card disclosure yet; Oklahoma is the benchmark, and Travis is best-positioned in Texas to be first.
